title: Putana, and why Krishna comes
hook: a lovely stranger brings poison to Nanda's house, and the baby she came to kill ends her
carry: an avatar comes to protect the good
tomorrow: the sweet smoke of Putana's pyre

segments.voice: Yesterday Yogamaya slipped from Kamsa's hands as the Goddess, the Lord's own power, and Kamsa chose fear and sent his people after newborns. Your line was shakti, divine power, worshiped as the Goddess.

Nanda is away in Mathura, paying his dues to the king, and Vasudeva, meeting him there, has warned him: go home quickly, there may be trouble in Gokula. Back in the village, a woman arrives. She is beautiful, the Bhagavata says, with flowers in her hair, a soft smile, a graceful walk. The cowherd women think a goddess has come to visit. She walks straight into Nanda's house, to the bed where the baby is lying.
screen: `NANDA IS AWAY.` → `A BEAUTIFUL STRANGER.` → `SHE WALKS TO THE BABY'S BED.`

segments.voice: Putana is one of Kamsa's killers. The Bhagavata calls her a demoness who goes from town to town killing infants, and today, by her magic, she has taken the form of a lovely woman. And the people guarding the child, Yashoda and Rohini, are so struck by her sweetness that they just stand there and watch her lift him. The danger doesn't break in. It's welcomed. Then the text turns the picture around: Putana takes the child on her lap the way someone picks up a sleeping snake, thinking it's a rope. As she comes near, the baby closes his eyes; the verse doesn't say why. She offers him her breast, smeared with poison. He feeds, and draws her very life out with it. She screams, let go, let go, and the earth shakes. As she dies, her disguise falls away, and her true body crashes down, crushing trees. On top of it, the cowherd women find the baby, playing, unafraid. Why does a baby god begin his life fighting demons? Krishna answers that himself, years later, in the Bhagavad Gita. Whenever dharma, the right order of things, falls apart, I come, age after age, to protect the good and to end the work of the wicked. Hindus call this coming down an avatar. Putana kills babies; the first thing the infant Krishna does is stop her. In Hindu teaching, that's what the Lord's coming is for: to stand with the ones who can't protect themselves.
screen: `A KILLER IN A LOVELY FORM` · `THE MOTHERS JUST WATCH` · `"LET GO, LET GO"` · then, large: `AVATAR: HE COMES TO PROTECT THE GOOD`

segments.voice: Many Hindus keep one name of Krishna close for hard moments: Krishna, or Govinda, a name from his childhood among the cowherds. Bring to mind one person who can't easily protect themselves: a small child, an elder, someone being picked on. Say the name quietly a few times, holding them in mind. If you don't pray, hold them in steady good wishes, and notice one small way you could stand on their side this week.
Putana. A killer sent by Kamsa, who comes to the baby as a beautiful woman with poison, and whose life he draws out.
Your line: an avatar comes to protect the good. Tomorrow, what the village finds when it burns Putana's body. Day eight hundred eighty-five, done.

screen: `DAY 885 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SWEET SMOKE OF PUTANA'S PYRE.`

howItsDone: The killing of Putana is told in the Bhagavata Purana's tenth book and is one of the childhood episodes Hindus retell in songs, dance-dramas and temple art; Hindus call each such coming of the Lord to earth an avatar.

Putana.meaning: a demoness sent by Kamsa to kill infants

Nanda.meaning: the cowherd of Gokula, Krishna's foster father

Rohini.meaning: Vasudeva's other wife, Balarama's mother, in Gokula

Gokula.meaning: the cowherd village where Krishna is hidden

Mathura.meaning: Kamsa's city, where Nanda pays his dues

avatar.meaning: the Lord's coming down to earth in a form

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.5.20–32: Nanda goes to Mathura, Vasudeva's warning
Bhagavata Purana 10.6.1–18: Putana's arrival, the women's reaction, the poisoned breast, her death in her true form
Bhagavad Gita 4.7–8: whenever dharma declines, the Lord comes age after age to protect the good and destroy wrongdoing

notes: All paraphrase; 'let go, let go' glosses her cry (10.6.11), not a quotation of a translation.
Confirm: the women take her for a goddess (the text compares her to Shri); the child closes his eyes; the snake-and-rope simile; Yashoda and Rohini watch, overcome by her beauty.
The text gives a size for Putana's fallen body (trees crushed over a distance); the number is left out.
Commentators give reasons why the child closed his eyes; the script names two as possibilities without attributing them. Confirm the verse does not itself give a reason.
Editor pass: corrected the snake-and-rope simile: in the Bhagavata the sleeping snake is the child Putana picks up, not Putana herself.
